newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Menem plays down talk of U.S. role over Falklands.
newsitem.headline: Menem plays down talk of U.S. role over Falklands.

text.p: Argentine President Carlos Menem played down on Monday a newspaper report that he would ask U.S. President Bill Clinton to mediate in Argentina's dispute with Britain over the Falkland Islands.

Argentina's biggest-selling newspaper Clarin said on Monday the Peronist leader would make the request during Clinton's visit to Argentina planned for March. Menem already raised the issue on a visit to Washington in December.
But Menem, asked in a radio interview whether the report was true, said: "No, this is a version possibly based on what I said in my last meeting with President Clinton."

The Argentine president clarified that what he was seeking from Clinton was "some sort of decision about trying to help us on the issue of sovereignty" -- and said he made the same request to Clinton's predecessor George Bush.
The United States, then under President Ronald Reagan, stood by its NATO ally Britain during the bloody 10-week war with Argentina over the remote South Atlantic islands in 1982.
About 1,000 soldiers, mostly Argentine, died and Argentina lost the war. But it maintains its claim to the islands which it calls Malvinas and says were "usurped" by Britain in 1833.

Since Menem came to power in 1989, Argentina has resumed diplomatic ties with Britain, hosted visits by British royals and forged trade links. Menem has insisted he will win back the islands by 2000 while agreeing to put sovereignty under a diplomatic "umbrella" to allow progress on other issues.

In the face of Britain's dogged refusal to even discuss the issue of sovereignty, the government has had to defend its "charm policy" aimed at winning over the islanders, while closing the diplomatic "umbrella".
"That famous 'umbrella' to not talk about sovereignty is now closed for good," Menem said at the weekend.

He is floating the idea of shared sovereignty and said on Monday: "Our intention now is to talk in principle, and not as a definitive solution, about some sort of shared sovereignty. But we will never renounce the issue of sovereignty."
Britain rejects any idea of shared rule of the islands.
